characterization_methods.purpose: Quantify the hardening effects of the different austenite decomposition reactions at the various processing conditions
Microstructural analysis of all alloys at the different processing conditions (hot-rolling and tempering)

analytical_models.equation_role: Predicts equilibrium phase fractions (in mol) as a function of temperature to assess the austenite (FCC_A1) stability gradient between the hot-rolling (1150 °C) and tempering (800 °C) equilibria
analytical_models.model_name: Equilibrium phase-amount vs temperature diagram for 9Al-30Mn-1C (Fig. 12(b))
analytical_models.model_note: Legend for Fig. 12(b): FCC_A1, BCC_2SL, LIQUID, KAPPA_E21, BCC_A2. The calculation shows austenite is more stable at 800 °C than at 1150 °C for this composition.

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: The alloyed steels were produced by casting using a 100 kW vacuum induction furnace, resulting in 0.5 kg ingots.
Ingots were hot-rolled at 1150 °C to obtain 5 mm flat products, followed by water quenching. This is the parent process (proc_hot-rolled-1150c) of the 800 °C tempering.

processing_steps.method: tempering at 800 °C followed by water quenching
processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Samples were heat treated at 600 °C and 800 °C for 30 min, followed by water quenching; conclusions state that tempering at 800 °C triggered complete and widespread transformations (cellular transformation coupled with spinodal decomposition).

measurement_conditions.test_standard: Vickers macro-hardness, 5 kg load, 5 indentations per sample

structures.overall_structure: No direct micrograph or EDS is reported specifically for 9Al-30Mn-1C at 800 °C. The alloy falls within the general finding that 800 °C tempering of these Fe–Mn–Al–C grades triggered complete and widespread transformations, i.e. cellular transformation coupled with spinodal decomposition, and that spinodal decomposition becomes more significant as Mn (austenite stability) increases, occurring at the expense of cellular transformation. The CALPHAD phase-fraction diagram for this composition (Fig. 12(b)) shows the austenite (FCC_A1) fraction is higher (more stable) at 800 °C than at 1150 °C, indicating a smaller thermodynamic driving force for austenite decomposition than in the 12Al grades.

unmapped_findings: No optical or SEM micrograph and no EDS table is reported specifically for 9Al-30Mn-1C tempered at 800 °C (Table 6 EDS is for 9Al-10Mn-1C at 800 °C and Table 7/Fig. 7-8 for 12Al-20Mn-1C at 800 °C); the 800 °C data for the 9Al-30Mn-1C alloy in this paper are limited to the Table 8 Vickers hardness (238 HV) and the CALPHAD phase-fraction diagram in Fig. 12(b).

For 9Al-30Mn-1C the CALPHAD austenite (FCC_A1) fraction is higher (indicating greater stability) at 800 °C than at 1150 °C — the opposite of the 12Al-20/30Mn-1C alloys — which the authors use to explain why the 9Al alloys decomposed less readily on tempering.

The hardening increment of 9Al-30Mn-1C on 800 °C tempering (216 → 238 HV) is smaller than on 600 °C tempering (216 → 330 HV), and the table discussion notes the hardening increment relative to the hot-rolled state shrinks as Mn rises from 10 to 30 wt%.

The authors note that the 12% Al alloys (12Al-10Mn-1C, 12Al-20Mn-1C, 12Al-30Mn-1C) are the ones that underwent full/reactions involving the whole austenite volume at 800 °C; for the 9Al-30Mn-1C grade no such reaction extent is reported explicitly.
